Good morning again from Green Valley Park in the Midlands, where Ridgegate won the toss, chose to field, and arrived with every reason to believe they could pull Southmoor back into the same kind of nervous, low-scoring struggle that had defined the previous meeting, yet this time the match took a very different shape because Southmoor finally found what both sides had been missing for most of this little sequence: one proper top-order innings that understood the surface, understood the match, and stayed long enough to give every later over a purpose. Oliver Clark was the reason. He did not turn the first half of the innings into a rush, and that was the important part, because the pitch still had that awkward Green Valley feel where the ball held just enough, stopped just enough, and made cross-batted impatience look dangerous. Martin Reed was scratchy beside him, almost painfully slow at times, but his stay gave Southmoor a platform they had not enjoyed often enough in this rivalry. The first stand crawled, paused, restarted, and kept taking the free runs Ridgegate kept leaving around the pads and outside the hitting arc. It was not glamorous cricket. It was useful cricket. The opening pair moved Southmoor to fifty-eight before Martin was finally trapped in front by Christopher Bell, and the hidden value of that stand was that it forced Ridgegate to bowl deep into the innings without the reward of a cluster. Oliver had made only part of the stand himself, the extras had helped heavily, Martin had soaked up balls, and Ridgegate still had no way to say the toss had worked. Brian Vale came in and did not last long, run out by Marcus Hale after a short maintenance partnership, but by then Oliver had shifted from survival into control. Kevin Garcia then gave the innings its real kick. He did not need long. A boundary, one clean strike over the rope, and suddenly the field looked less tight than it had half an hour earlier. That partnership with Oliver was the hinge of the innings, because it moved Southmoor from a careful score into a defensible one and made Ridgegate’s earlier leakage look expensive rather than merely untidy. Garcia’s run-out at one hundred and thirteen gave Ridgegate a brief opening, but Oliver had already reached the phase where the bowling no longer looked as if it could own him. Elliot Martinez stayed with him for the last push, and Oliver’s final burst, before John Vale finally bowled him near the end, carried the innings to a very different emotional place. Southmoor closed on one hundred and thirty-seven for five, and in a where the surface never looked fully kind, that felt more than competitive. The total had one real spine, Oliver’s seventy-two from fifty-nine, six boundaries and three blows over the top, but it also had the right small supports: Martin’s time, Garcia’s sharp burst, Elliot’s little finish, and a large but decisive extras column that kept Ridgegate from tightening the match in the middle. Ridgegate’s bowlers were not poor across the board. John Vale was tidy and removed the main man. Christopher Bell gave them the first wicket. Robert Mills held a reasonable line. The problem was that the attack never found the double strike that makes a slow opening stand look foolish, and once Richard Lane and William Cross leaked at the wrong end of the innings, Southmoor had the cushion they needed. Chasing one hundred and thirty-eight, Ridgegate needed a clean start or at least one calm, extended partnership. They got neither for long enough. Robert Mills struck a boundary and looked briefly positive, but Andrew Lee had him caught behind with only twelve on the board, and that early wicket immediately made the chase feel less like a measured pursuit and more like another one of those low-score traps. William Cross and John Vale then produced Ridgegate’s best passage, a stand of twenty-eight that did not dominate but did at least give the innings a recognisable shape. John Vale made sixteen, William stayed long enough to suggest he might anchor the reply, and for a while the target looked manageable if not comfortable. Ronald Bell broke that calm by removing John, and after that Southmoor began to squeeze with a clarity Ridgegate had failed to find in the first innings. Marcus Hale came and went cheaply. Richard Lane briefly hit with intent, but George King removed him before that little spark could become momentum. Daniel Stone fell almost immediately after. William Cross, who had been holding the innings together more by presence than command, was bowled with Ridgegate only in the mid-sixties, and in that moment the chase effectively cracked. Joseph Turner and Thomas Reed disappeared in the same lower-order pressure wave, and at sixty-six for eight the target was no longer the main opponent. The opponent was panic. George King’s spell was the heart of that collapse, five wickets for very little, not just tail-end leftovers but the dismissals that kept Ridgegate from stitching together any late repair. Ronald Bell’s two wickets mattered in the middle. Paul Carter’s quick strike on Marcus Hale helped remove the captain before he could reset the chase. Jonah Walker later got Christopher Bell to shut down one more small partnership. Joshua Walker and Steven Wright did add some late dignity, and their final stand at least made Southmoor bowl out the full distance instead of walking through the last few overs untouched, but it never felt like a chase coming back to life. It felt like a scorecard being rescued from complete collapse. Joshua finished unbeaten, Steven flicked one late blow, and Ridgegate reached ninety-two for nine, still forty-five short and never close enough in the final quarter to put real stress back on Southmoor. That is the clearest difference between the two innings. Southmoor had one batter who stayed long enough to organize the entire card. Ridgegate had fragments. Southmoor’s best stand became a platform and then their third stand became acceleration. Ridgegate’s best stand became only a temporary pause before the middle caved in. Southmoor’s extras helped them build a total; Ridgegate’s extras only softened the defeat. So the result, Southmoor by forty-five runs and winners, felt properly earned. Oliver Clark was the obvious player of the match because his innings changed the whole tone of the contest. On a day when almost everyone else batted in pieces, he produced the one complete hand: patient enough to survive the slow start, strong enough to lift the death overs, and clear enough in judgment to turn a difficult surface into a winning score.

Aria Stone was already alert in the ring, moving in before the batters had committed, and when Kaya was caught short the innings tipped from difficult into fully damaged. Crest Women never found a phase they could own. Willow Women owned almost all of them.

At Mariner's Oval in Southport, Pearlbridge Women chose to field first, and for the first few overs the decision did not look reckless because Cresthaven Women were moving forward without yet looking completely loose. Elena Brooks found a couple of clean scoring strokes and Ava Morgan gave the opening stand a practical shape, but Pearlbridge still had enough early control to believe the innings could be kept within reach. The first breakthrough came when Ruby Knox had Elena caught, and although Cresthaven had already reached a useful base, the dismissal still offered Pearlbridge the chance to drag the scoring back before the middle overs opened. That chance did not last. Tara Finch arrived and immediately gave Cresthaven a different attacking profile. She was not simply swinging through the line; she was choosing her areas carefully, punishing width, leaning into anything full, and making every loose delivery feel expensive. Ava stayed long enough to help the second stand grow, but Lena Ward removed her before that partnership could become the whole story. At that stage Pearlbridge had two wickets and a workable position on paper, yet the match was about to move decisively away from them because Tara and Mira Carter built the stand that defined the innings. Tara supplied the visible pressure, the boundaries, the tempo, the sense that Pearlbridge’s bowlers could not miss by much without paying. Mira was less noisy at first and then increasingly severe, building her innings with a calmer rhythm before accelerating once the field spread. Their partnership was worth eighty-five, and it did not feel like one sudden burst so much as a steady taking-over of the game. Pearlbridge kept trying to reset with different bowlers, but the problem was that their discipline cracked too often. Wides kept appearing at the wrong moments, a couple of no-balls kept the batting side fed, and even when one over began neatly, the finish too often gave Cresthaven the release they needed. Ruby Knox did eventually come back to remove Tara for sixty-four, and that wicket prevented the innings from becoming completely unbroken through the final quarter. But by then the damage had already been done. Mira was set, the total was already moving toward a heavy range, and the batting side had enough resources left to keep pressing. Sienna Park fell quickly to Farah Noor, which gave Pearlbridge a second late interruption, yet Rowan Vale came in and played the small finishing role correctly. She did not need a major innings with the bat. She needed to keep Mira on strike, run hard, take the loose ball when it came, and make sure the last overs did not stall after the two quick breaks. Mira finished unbeaten on sixty-six, a compact but forceful innings that gave Cresthaven their permanent center after Tara departed. Rowan added a brief unbeaten hand, and Cresthaven closed on one hundred and eighty-four for four, a total built through layers rather than one isolated hit. Elena and Ava gave the base, Tara gave the acceleration, Mira gave the long finish, and Rowan made sure the closing phase stayed clean. Pearlbridge’s bowling had moments of value, especially Ruby’s two wickets and the control Mira Khan briefly found, but the attack as a whole never held pressure long enough. The extras were not a side note. They repeatedly turned half-decent overs into profitable ones and made a strong batting performance look heavier. Chasing one hundred and eighty-five required an exceptional start, and Pearlbridge got almost the worst possible one. Rowan Vale struck with the first ball, bowling Aisha Reed before the reply had any rhythm, and that single moment changed the emotional direction of the chase. Riya Noor tried to survive with Nia Grant, but the innings was already in repair mode, and Pippa Lane removed Riya before Pearlbridge could build a true opening stand. Lena Ward then came in and became the only batter who looked capable of resisting the collapse for any length of time. She did not dominate in a chase sense because the target was too large and the wickets kept falling around her, but she did stay, and that mattered because without her the innings would have ended much earlier. Nia Grant gave a small amount of support before Ruby North had her caught by Clara Moss, and once that wicket fell Pearlbridge entered the decisive collapse. Rowan returned and cut straight through the middle. Ruby Knox was bowled, Maya Wells was pinned in front, and suddenly the chase had gone from difficult to nearly impossible. The score had barely moved from the mid-twenties, and half the side was gone. Farah Noor tried to stand with Lena for a few overs, but Ava Reed removed her before any real repair could form. Then Rowan struck again, first bowling Mina Stone, then trapping Sara Vale, and the match was effectively over with Pearlbridge eight down and still nowhere near respectability. What made Rowan’s spell so damaging was not just the number of wickets. It was the timing. Tessa Lane hung around briefly before Elena Brooks bowled her, leaving Lena with only the last pair. Olivia Shore then gave the innings its final small pocket of resistance, not enough to threaten anything, but enough to prevent the chase from ending in complete silence. Lena kept taking what was available, found boundaries when Cresthaven finally missed fuller, and dragged the total to sixty before Olivia was run out by Jade Flint. That final wicket ended the reply in the seventeenth over, and the margin of one hundred and twenty-four runs reflected the actual gap between the sides. Pearlbridge, by contrast, had one batter standing and almost nothing around her. Lena’s unbeaten thirty-nine was a captain’s effort in the narrowest and hardest sense: not control, not a chase-shaping hand, just defiance inside a chase that had already collapsed. That is why Rowan Vale’s Player of the Match award fits cleanly. Tara Finch and Mira Carter shaped the match with the bat, and either would have been central in an ordinary win, but Rowan’s spell made sure the defence became a rout rather than a contest. Cresthaven built the heavier innings, accepted the extras Pearlbridge offered, then used the new ball and middle overs to turn scoreboard pressure into wickets. Pearlbridge were beaten by the size of the target first, then by the speed with which their chase lost structure, and finally by a five-wicket burst that removed any possibility of late resistance becoming meaningful.

They completed the seventy-five-run stand in only eight overs and two balls, Seabrook closing on seventy-five for one, and the nine-wicket margin accurately captured the gulf between the two innings. Meadowfield had Evelyn Brooks’ resistance, Iris Moore’s small late push, and a single early wicket in the defense; Seabrook had the decisive bowling spell, the tighter fielding shape, and the only truly commanding batting partnership of the match.
